title: External Sorting & Aggregation
short: Sorting when the data exceeds RAM
lead: Sort a file without holding it all in RAM, then ask whether the query needs order or only a small state for each group.
goals: Connect query execution to the implementation of individual operators
Calculate the number of passes in two-way and multiway external merge sort
Compare reading through clustered and unclustered B+ trees

sections.title: Sort a file that cannot fit in memory
sections.html:
The shop asks for orders in amount order. If the file is bigger than RAM, “load it all and sort” is not an executable plan. We can, however, sort a portion that fits and save that portion to disk. Such a sorted sequence is called a run. If we can merge sorted runs using little memory, the complete file need never fit at once. This is external sorting: the algorithm explicitly plans transfers between RAM and storage instead of relying on unpredictable virtual-memory paging.

First see why merging works. Take sorted runs A=[1,4,4] and B=[2,4,7]. Only their current first unconsumed values can be the smallest remaining value. Compare the two heads, emit the smaller, and advance only its input.

Heads A / BEmitOutput so far
1 / 21 from A[1]
4 / 22 from B[1,2]
4 / 44 from A (tie policy)[1,2,4]
4 / 44 from A[1,2,4,4]
empty / 44 from B[1,2,4,4,4]
empty / 77 from B[1,2,4,4,4,7]

Sorting keeps all three copies of 4. DISTINCT would add a separate step keeping one representative of adjacent equals, yielding [1,2,4,7]. GROUP BY could combine the equal-key group’s values instead. ORDER BY, duplicate elimination, grouping, merge joins and bulk index loading can therefore use sorting for different purposes. With multiple sort columns, compare the first column; only ties compare the next. For (city,amount), (A,30) precedes (B,10) because A precedes B, even though 30>10. This is lexicographic order.

At page scale, keep one input frame per run and one output frame. When an input frame is consumed, read its next page; when output fills, write it. The head comparison needs current pages, not every page of both runs. Now we can count the complete file transfers.

sections.title: Count runs before writing the logarithm
sections.html:
Use an original file of N=90 pages and B=6 one-page frames. Count page reads and writes, ignore CPU, and write the final sorted file to disk. Pass 0 reads six pages, sorts them in RAM, writes a six-page run, then repeats. It creates 90/6=15 runs. For merging, reserve one output frame, leaving five input frames: merge up to B−1=5 runs at a time.

PassRuns enteringRuns leavingRead + write I/O
0: sort RAM batchesUnsorted 90 pages15 runs of 6 pages90+90=180
1: merge groups of 515 runs3 runs of 30 pages90+90=180
2: merge remaining 33 runs1 run of 90 pages90+90=180

Thus the run counts are 15→3→1, with three passes including pass 0; cost=180+180+180=540 I/Os. In general pass 0 makes ceil(N/B) runs. Each later pass divides the run count by at most B−1, rounding up. For N>0 and B≥3 the total is 1+ceil(log_(B−1)(ceil(N/B))) passes, and materialising every pass costs 2N times that count. The initial 1 is pass 0, not another merge. The lecture’s simpler two-way variant makes one-page runs and merges pairs, giving 1+ceil(log₂N). It uses its buffers less effectively than the general B-frame version.

If 0<N≤B, pass 0 already creates one run: one read and final write, 2N I/Os. Empty input needs no data-page sorting I/O. Streaming the last sorted output directly to its consumer can avoid the final N-page write; do not subtract a reread that was never in this sorting cost. DISTINCT or aggregation may reduce output size, so their passes need separate accounting.

Before sorting, ask whether an existing B+ tree already provides the requested order. Record-containing leaves can be scanned directly. A clustered reference index adds data fetches with useful locality; an unclustered reference index may chase a different page for every tuple. Count index pages and data pages separately. Ordered index entries do not guarantee cheap ordered full-row output.

Key takeaway

Count the runs and passes before substituting into a formula. Pipelining the final output directly into the next operator may avoid the final write, but state that assumption before subtracting any I/O.

sections.title: Aggregate by updating a small state
sections.html:
The manager changes the question to average sale per region. We do not need every order retained after contributing to its group. For original rows (North,10), (South,8), (North,14), keep a table mapping each region to (sum,count). It is a temporary hash table used by this operator, not necessarily an index stored with the base data.

Row readNorth stateSouth state
Before inputabsentabsent
(North,10)(10,1)absent
(South,8)(10,1)(8,1)
(North,14)(24,2)(8,1)
Output average24/2=128/1=8

SUM,COUNT,MIN and MAX likewise keep running state. DISTINCT stores which keys have been seen and discards further copies. To combine two partial averages, combine sums and counts, then divide; averaging the two averages can be wrong when their counts differ. For North’s two rows and South’s one row, overall mean is (24+8)/(2+1)=32/3, not (12+8)/2=10.

What if there are too many distinct groups for the state to fit? Use one input frame and B−1 output frames to partition tuples by group key onto disk. Equal group keys must enter the same partition. Process partitions one at a time, building an in-memory table with a hash distinction independent of the partition function. All keys in one partition already share its partition address; reusing only that address would not distribute them inside the table. If a partition’s state still does not fit, repartition with another suitable independent function.

Fit concerns state plus hash-table overhead, not just input pages. An idealised B−1 equal partitions, each fitting about B pages of state, suggests capacity about B(B−1) pages. It is a rough bound, not a guarantee. For N=90,B=10 and expansion factor f=1.2, each average partition needs 1.2×90/9=12 state pages, already more than ten. Skew can make one partition worse still. Rehashing cannot separate identical keys; a million copies of one SUM key should be combined into its small state instead. These row-count, state-size and distribution questions must be checked before applying an external-hashing cost.

Key takeaway

To combine averages, keep both the sum and the count. When two groups have different row counts, averaging their two averages does not give the combined average.

sections.title: Decide whether order is part of the answer
sections.html:
Compare two requests: DISTINCT customer_id, and DISTINCT customer_id ORDER BY customer_id. Both remove repeated IDs, but only the second promises key order. Hashing is a candidate for the first. Sorting can satisfy both duplicate adjacency and final order for the second. Neither SQL DISTINCT nor GROUP BY alone promises sorted output. Existing order, distinct-group count, available memory, I/O and CPU costs can change the choice.

Recalculate the 90-page sort with ten frames, writing the final result. Explain where every pass comes from.

Reasoned answer. Pass 0 creates ceil(90/10)=9 sorted runs. One output frame leaves nine input frames, so a single merge combines all nine. Two passes cost 2×90×2=360 I/Os. With six frames the sequence was 15→3→1 and 540 I/Os; four additional frames removed a complete read/write pass, rather than merely making every comparison faster.

A million rows all have customer_id=7. Does a DISTINCT hash table necessarily need a million stored entries? Would another partition hash split that one key?

Reasoned answer. No: DISTINCT can retain one entry for 7 and discard duplicates. Another key-based partition hash still sends every 7 to the same partition. For aggregation, keep the appropriate state; for a raw join, preserving duplicate tuples has different semantics, as the next lesson shows.

Use the sorting lab to change run counts and compare its I/O totals. Each displayed number represents one whole page containing one key, so it makes page transfers visible rather than modelling variable tuple sizes. Its B-frame initial runs are the general multiway variant, not the one-page initial runs of the lecture’s basic two-way example.

quiz.question: For N=90 and B=6, how many I/Os does multiway sorting require when the final output is written?
quiz.explanation: Pass 0 reads and writes 90 pages and creates 15 runs. Five input frames plus one output frame merge them into 3 runs, then 1. These are three complete passes, each 90 reads+90 writes=180 I/Os: 3×180=540, including the final sorted-file write.
